children: The last time the European Central Bank changed presidents in the middle of a hiking cycle, the new chief cut rates
Euro zone leaders just picked the man who will face the same test in 2027.
Leaders meeting in Brussels on Thursday backed
Pablo Hernández de Cos
, general manager of the Bank for International Settlements and governor of the Bank of Spain from 2018 to 2024, to succeed
Christine Lagarde
. He would become the first Spaniard to run the ECB since its creation in 1998.
Lagarde
leaves on Feb. 7, 2027, almost nine months early. The Netherlands dropped its push for former Dutch central bank chief
Klaas Knot
, clearing the way.
A Pragmatist With a Dovish Tilt
Frederik Ducrozet
, head of macroeconomic research at Pictet Wealth Management, described the pick as a vote for stability.
“A trained, experienced, pragmatic central banker who should ensure policy continuity, central bank independence, and consensus-based decision making,” Ducrozet said in a post on X.
Matthew Ryan
, head of market strategy at Ebury, saw the same continuity, with one difference in emphasis.

“The choice of Hernández de Cos to replace Christine Lagarde at the helm of the ECB is a mildly dovish one,” Ryan said in emailed comments. “A Draghi ally with a supervisory background, he is likely to place greater weight on growth, financial stability and fragmentation risk than Klaas Knot, the alternative candidate and a genuine hawk.”
Fragmentation risk is the danger that one country’s borrowing costs break away from the rest, making a single interest rate for 21 countries hard to run.
November 2011: The Handover That Flipped the Script
In April and July 2011,
Jean-Claude Trichet
raised the ECB’s main refinancing rate to 1.5%.
Mario Draghi
took over on Nov. 1, 2011, as Italian and Spanish bond yields spiraled. Two days later, at his first meeting, he cut rates. A second cut followed in December, unwinding Trichet’s tightening.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, and euro zone inflation hit 4% in October, twice the bank’s target.
However, Ryan does not expect a Draghi-style reversal.

“The president sets the agenda but is ultimately one voice on the Governing Council, and rarely overrides the consensus,” he said. Ebury still sees a December hike as its base case, followed by a prolonged pause.
Pantheon Macroeconomics chief eurozone economist
Claus Vistesen

also expects a quarter-point hike in December, with March a closer call. In a note this week, Pantheon said that if French bonds sell off again, the ECB would more likely step in through its balance sheet than abandon further hikes, as long as inflation stays high.
Bonds Did Not Price a Dove
Germany’s two-year yield, the most sensitive to rate expectations, rose 2 basis points to 3.08% on Thursday, while the 10-year Bund climbed 4 basis points to 3.26%.
The euro held near $1.0975, down 6.5% against the dollar this year, a slide tracked by the
Invesco CurrencyShares Euro Trust
Equities rallied for other reasons, as tariff worries eased and tech rebounded. The Euro Stoxx 50 jumped 2.2% to 6,026.55. The
SPDR EURO STOXX 50 ETF
is still down 3.7% this year in dollar terms.
Politicians welcomed the choice. “Fast and good choice,” former Italian Prime Minister
Enrico Letta
said on X.
Fast and good choice. The new
🇪🇺President is Pablo Henrnadez De Cos.
Spanish Prime Minister
Pedro Sánchez
called it a sign of “a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before.”
Un español al frente del Banco Central Europeo.
Una española al frente de la Vicepresidencia primera de la Comisión Europea.
Una española al frente del Banco Europeo de Inversiones.
En resumen, una España que lidera en Europa como nunca lo había hecho.
The formal appointment still lies ahead. The bigger question comes after it: whether the man picked for continuity will, like Draghi, be tested in his first weeks.

title: Pablo Hernández de Cos Gets the ECB Job: Analysts Call It Continuity — With a Twist
